strengths: Addresses a key limitation of VLMs (lack of fine-grained visual localization) by fusing them with the rich visual priors of VFMs (like DINOv2) in a training-free transductive zero-shot learning paradigm.

The proposed OTFusion framework is theoretically elegant, casting the joint semantic-visual alignment as an entropy-regularized Optimal Transport problem over GMM-derived and VLM-derived probability distributions.

Outstanding empirical performance across 11 diverse datasets, showing an average accuracy improvement of around 10% over the original CLIP and consistently outperforming recent transductive and test-time adaptation methods.
The method is highly scalable and model-agnostic, capable of easily integrating multiple visual or language foundation models without retraining or architecture modifications.
weaknesses: The paper operates under the transductive setting, assuming the entire unlabeled test set is available at once. Its performance under small batches, streaming/online test-time adaptation, or highly unbalanced class distributions is not explored.

A quantitative discussion on the computational complexity and runtime overhead (e.g., as a function of dataset size $N$ and class count $C$) is missing, which is important since GMM fitting and Sinkhorn iterations are performed at test time.

Hyperparameter selection (e.g., $\lambda$) seems to affect some datasets significantly (such as EuroSAT and Flowers102, as seen in Figure 2). It is not fully clear if a single set of hyperparameters is used across all datasets, or how they would be tuned without access to labeled validation data in a zero-shot setting.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: combining the rich visual representations of Vision-only Foundation Models (VFMs like DINOv2) with the strong semantic alignment of Vision-Language Models (VLMs like CLIP) for transductive zero-shot learning.
The proposed OTFusion is fully training-free and plug-and-play, making it highly efficient to deploy in resource-constrained scenarios without any parameter fine-tuning.
Extensive experiments on 11 standard image classification benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over native CLIP and several recent transductive and test-time adaptation baselines.
The paper is well-written, with clear mathematical formulations, intuitive t-SNE visualizations, and comprehensive parameter sensitivity and convergence analyses.
weaknesses: A major weakness is shown in the ablation study (Table 2): the naive 'Concatenation' baseline (concatenating CLIP and DINOv2 features and then running the GMM-based transduction) actually outperforms the proposed OTFusion (75.54% vs 74.95% on average). Since a simpler feature-level fusion strategy achieves better performance, it weakens the motivation for the more complex distribution-level Optimal Transport fusion.

The authors claim that concatenation is less scalable than OTFusion as the number of foundation models ($K$) increases. However, no quantitative evidence (e.g., latency, memory consumption, or scaling curves) is provided to back up this claim. A rigorous complexity and execution time comparison between Concatenation and OTFusion is missing.

The methodological novelty relative to TransCLIP (Zanella et al., NeurIPS 2024) is somewhat incremental. TransCLIP already introduced the GMM and Optimal Transport formulation for transductive CLIP adaptation. OTFusion essentially extends this by adding a second feature source (DINOv2), but the underlying optimization framework remains very similar.

The transductive setting assumes access to the entire test set at once. The paper lacks an analysis of how the performance of OTFusion scales or degrades when the size of the unlabeled test set is small (e.g., batch-size sensitivity), which is a common limitation of transductive methods in real-world streaming applications.

strengths: Strong motivation and elegant framework: Bridging the complementary benefits of visually discriminative, self-supervised Vision-only Foundation Models (VFMs) and semantically aligned Vision-Language Models (VLMs) via a training-free probabilistic optimal transport framework is highly intuitive and well-formulated.

Exceptional empirical results: The proposed OTFusion delivers substantial accuracy improvements (+10.17% on average with CLIP-ViT/B16 and +11.77% with ResNet50) across 11 diverse datasets compared to the baseline zero-shot CLIP. It also consistently outperforms recent transductive state-of-the-art methods such as TransCLIP (NeurIPS 2024) and ECALP (ICLR 2025).

Highly detailed and comprehensive evaluation: The paper includes a thorough ablation study verifying individual components, parameter sensitivity analyses (for the entropy regularization parameter $\epsilon$ and the fusion coefficient $\lambda$), and convergence curves demonstrating rapid stabilization within 3 to 5 iterations.
weaknesses: Unclear novelty distinction over TransCLIP: The formulation of transductive classification using a GMM combined with entropy-regularized optimal transport solved via the Sinkhorn algorithm is conceptually very similar to TransCLIP (Zanella et al., NeurIPS 2024). The paper would be much stronger if it explicitly highlighted the mathematical and algorithmic differences between OTFusion and TransCLIP beyond simply adding a third term for the VFM distribution.

Performance vs. Concatenation: In Table 2, the 'Concatenation' baseline (concatenating CLIP and DINOv2 features together and feeding them into the pipeline) actually achieves an average accuracy of 75.54%, which is slightly higher than the proposed OTFusion (74.95%). Although the paper mentions that feature concatenation incurs high computational and memory overhead, no concrete quantitative analysis (such as runtime or memory consumption comparison) is provided to justify the trade-off.

Inconsistent mathematical notation: There is some confusion in the notation. The number of classes is defined as $C$ in the Preliminary section, but later referred to as $K$ in Equations (4) and (5). Additionally, in Equation (6), the summation index is $i$ (for aggregating over different models), but $i$ is also used as the sample index (from $1$ to $N$) throughout the paper, which makes the notation confusing.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework: The paper systematically addresses the integration of heterogeneous foundation models (both Vision-Language Models like CLIP and Vision-only Models like DINO) to leverage their complementary semantic and visual strengths.

Solid mathematical formulation: It formulates the multi-model ensemble problem as a self-adaptive optimal transport (OT) problem. The introduction of the squared inner product enables automatic weight estimation without labels, solved elegantly using a Minorization-Maximization (MM) scheme.

Thorough empirical validation: The method is comprehensively evaluated on 26 distinct datasets spanning three diverse domains (natural images, remote sensing, and medical pathology). The results show outstanding improvement margins over state-of-the-art transductive and test-time adaptation baselines.
Practical and training-free: SOTA does not require weight fine-tuning or access to internal model weights, making it highly applicable to black-box models available only through APIs.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to batch size / dataset scale: Since the method relies on fitting GMMs and solving OT on unlabeled target data, it is unclear how robust SOTA is when the number of target samples is extremely small (e.g., in online test-time adaptation settings with small batch sizes).

Hyperparameter analysis: The paper could benefit from a more detailed sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters, such as the entropy regularization $\epsilon$ and the softmax temperature $\tau$, across different domains.

Inference overhead: Although shown to be more efficient than graph-based methods, running multi-model feature extraction and iterative optimization inevitably increases inference latency and memory requirements compared to single-model inference.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and elegant framework (SOTA) that integrates multiple foundation models (VFMs and VLMs) using self-adaptive optimal transport, exploiting the semantic alignment of VLMs and the fine-grained discriminative power of VFMs.

The proposed formulation is training-free and prior-free. It uses a quadratic objective function solved via Minorization-Maximization (MM) and the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm to adaptively weight the contribution of each model without relying on any ground-truth validation labels.

Extensive experimental validation across 26 datasets in three distinct domains (natural, remote sensing, medical pathology) demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over state-of-the-art test-time adaptation and transductive methods.
The paper is well-written, with high-quality visualizations (e.g., t-SNE and clustering comparison radar charts) and a comprehensive ablation study that validates each key component of the design.
weaknesses: The transductive setting assumes that the entire unlabeled target dataset is available at once. While the authors also present an inductive setting, both settings still rely on a reasonably sized batch of unlabeled data to reliably estimate GMM parameters, which might limit its applicability in streaming or sample-by-sample real-time scenarios.
There is a minor notation typo in Eq. (19) on page 9, where $Q^{(t)}_{ic}$ is used in the denominator instead of $T^{(k+1)}_{ic}$. This should be corrected for clarity.

The paper would benefit from a discussion on how the number of classes $K$ and the scale of the dataset affect the optimization time and memory footprint, as well as the sensitivity to the entropy parameter $\epsilon$.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: how to effectively ensemble multiple foundation models (VLMs and VFMs) for zero-shot classification without requiring training or fine-tuning.

The introduction of the quadratic objective in Eq. 7 to achieve self-adaptive model weighting, optimized via the Minorization-Maximization (MM) algorithm, is theoretically elegant and avoids manual hyperparameter tuning.
The authors evaluate the method on a large number of datasets (26 in total) across three distinct domains (natural, remote sensing, and medical pathology), showing consistent improvements.
weaknesses: Unfair Comparison with Single-Model Baselines: In Table 1 and Table 4, SOTA ensembles CLIP-1 and DINOv2/v3, which significantly outperforms other methods. However, all other baselines (GDA, ZLaP, TransCLIP, ECALP, ADAPT, GTA-CLIP) only use a single CLIP-1 model. To demonstrate the true value of the self-adaptive OT formulation, the authors must compare SOTA against simple ensembling baselines (e.g., average pooling of CLIP and DINOv3 predictions, or concatenation of features followed by clustering) using the exact same set of models. Currently, it is unclear how much of the performance gain comes from the advanced OT formulation versus simply adding a stronger model like DINOv3.

Robustness to Class Imbalance: The transductive optimal transport framework heavily relies on the target marginal distribution q. Typically, q is set to a uniform distribution, assuming that all classes are equally represented in the test set. If the test set has a highly skewed class distribution (which is common in real-world scenarios like medical pathology or remote sensing), forcing a uniform marginal constraint can lead to a large drop in performance. The paper does not analyze or discuss SOTA's behavior under class-imbalanced test sets.

Instability of GMM in High Dimensions: Fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on high-dimensional visual features (e.g., 1024-dimensional features from DINOv2-L) without any supervision can be extremely unstable and sensitive to initialization. The paper lacks details on how GMM parameters are initialized, whether any dimensionality reduction (such as PCA) is performed, and how the model avoids degenerate solutions (e.g., variance collapsing to zero) during joint optimization (Eq. 8).

Computational and Memory Overhead of Multiple Foundation Models: Although SOTA is training-free, performing inference requires extracting features from multiple massive foundation models (e.g., CLIP, DINOv2, DINOv3). This drastically increases the computational latency and GPU memory footprint during test time, making it less practical for real-time or resource-constrained applications. The complexity analysis in Sec 8.3 only covers the optimization step but ignores the heavy feature extraction cost of multiple models.
